messages.subject: how to factor in changing detectability in spatial distance
messages.subject_clean: how to factor in changing detectability in spatial distance
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
I am planning a survey to estimate abundance of Kori Bustards in 3 land use
types (parks, community-managed and unprotected areas), and due to the low
encounter rate planned to use spatial distance as that would enable me
maximally use the few observations. I plan to estimate Effective Strip Width
(ESW) and probability of detection (P) for each of strata (PA, WMA and
unprotected), using "post stratification" function within DISTANCE.

In Ch. 4 of Buckland et al. (Advanced sampling) the spatial models used
assume ESW and P are the same in each strata. However, I anticipate there
could be large variances + spatial patterning in P for one of the land use
types (unprotected areas), as the livestock stocking rates (which affects
vegetation cover) within these areas are variable. Towards the end of the
abovementioned Ch. caution is made to be aware of  such confounding factors,
and the advice is that we should "accommodate trend in detectability" using
relevant covariates.

In a nutshell,

1.       how does one go about this in practice, given that in the first
place the number of observations is likely to be very small and thus
modelling of the detection function poor (if at all possible), which is why
we went for spatial modelling?

2.       How much error/difference is to be expected from P derived from the
global data vs. P from unprotected area-only data? Any thresholds for what
signifies too large a gap to possibly suggest I should stick to the possibly
more correct - but also possibly very incorrect due to too few data points -
P from unprotected area data only? simple t-test?

3.       How can I check which P estimate is more accurate?

4.       Am I correct to assume that the difference in abundance brought out
by using covariates for the unprotected area P and none for the other areas
in negligible - and that somehow a comparison of the estimates obtained
using a P with and without covariate gives a measure of the influence of the
variable stocking rate on the birds' density? If so, how is this to be
quantified?

Regards,
Kabelo

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Kabelo Senyatso

PhD student

School of Environmental Sciences

University of East Anglia

Norwich NR4 7TJ

United Kingdom

Fax: +44 (0) 1603 591045

messages.body_plain:
Kabelo:

Lots of questions within your query.  But before dealing with all of
them, I wonder if you have opted for the proper approach.  Spatial
modelling is not intended to remedy difficulties posed by a small number
of detections.  Rather its use derives from making inference about
places where you did not sample by using a model to make that inference,
rather than using a sampling design to make that inference.  Researchers
find themselves in this situation when they do not employ a randomized
sampling design (e.g., using ferry routes in the sea).  The spatial
modelling can actually be quite 'data hungry' because they require
information on covariates (both where you sample, and were you do not)
to produce their estimates.

So perhaps rethink the decision to travel down the spatial modelling route.

 - Professor Lord Robert May
 - Carmen Fernandez
 - Jeff Laake
 - Darryl MacKenzie
 - Marc Mangel

messages.subject_clean: trouble shooting survey design
messages.body_plain:
Hi Scott,

The shape file containing the study area should have a single record in
it, and the linkID value for this record should be 1 (not "some large
integer").  This is because the global layer in the distance project has
only one record and the ID for the record in this layer is 1, so if you
use some other value it won't match the shapefile record with the record
in the Distance project.

If this doesn't work, send me the project (zipped up - see manual) to
dist...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk and I'll look at it.

Cheers,

  - Len Thomas

messages.body_plain:
Hi Scott,

The shape file containing the study area should have a single record in
it, and the linkID value for this record should be 1 (not "some large
integer").  This is because the global layer in the distance project has
only one record and the ID for the record in this layer is 1, so if you
use some other value it won't match the shapefile record with the record
in the Distance project.

If this doesn't work, send me the project (zipped up - see manual) to
dist...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk and I'll look at it.

Cheers,

  - Len Thomas

messages.subject: Re: density by sample and cluster size as covariate in MCDS
messages.subject_clean: density by sample and cluster size as covariate in MCDS
messages.body_plain:
Julia:

Good to hear that you are continuing your analysis after the Point Reyes
workshop.

You are right, there is no clear mention of the impossibility of
estimating density by sample when cluster size is used as a covariate
with the MRDS (you are partially solving this via your email, so it will
now appear in a search of the distance-sampling list archive).

But a hint about the nature of error appears in the warning messages
just above it.

** Warning: Cannot estimate encounter rate variance empirically when estimating encounter rate by sample. Sample level encounter rate variances set to zero. **

** Warning: When cluster size is a covariate, variance of the cluster size, density of individuals, and abundance estimates can only be obtained via the bootstrap. You have not specified the bootstrap variance option, so these variance estimates will not be produced. **

With cluster size as a covariate, estimates of variance for density (and
other things) can only be produced by bootstrapping.  But you have
requested density estimates at the sample level (essentially the lowest
level of resolution in your data).  This places you within a paradox.
There is effectively no lower level of data organization upon which the
bootstrapping can be conducted.  Hence, you would have no measures of
precision associated with the estimates you desire, and the programmers
of Distance have not permitted that.

messages.subject: z-test for point transects and clusters
messages.subject_clean: z-test for point transects and clusters
messages.body_plain:
Dear  List,  Dr. Buckland,

I wish to use a z-test to compare densities of lemurs in two habitat type=
s.
They share a common detection function, so I consulted the listserv and t=
ext
for options for dealing with this dependence. I wish to adapt the
information on p. 85 in Buckland et al. 2001 to point transect data when
objects are clusters.=20

 In a response to one post, Dr. Buckland provided the following informati=
on:

=93You need to first find the variance of D1/f(0) and of D2/f(0) -
i.e. variance of n_1/L_1 and of variance n_2/L_2 if you don't have
clusters.  If you have clusters, variance of n_1 . E^(s)/L_1 is found by
the delta method.  Variance of (D1-D2)/f(0) is then the sum of these
variances.  Now find variance of [(D1-D2)/f(0)]*f(0) =3D D1-D2 by the del=
ta
method.  z =3D (D1-D2)/sqrt[var(D1-D2)]=94

And in another he provided this helpful information:

=93A paragraph to cover this in the book might have been helpful - sorry!=

Simply obtain the 2 density estimates, D^_1 and D^_2, then
M^_1=3DD^_1/h^(0) and similarly for M^_2.  Then var(M^_i) is as given on
p86, and in eqn 109, replace f^(0) by h^(0) throughout.=94

Am I correct, then, to use the following equation for M^_i for my point
transect data when objects are in clusters?

M^_i=3D((D^_i)(E^_i(s)))/h^(0)

Thank you,

Anne Axel

--

messages.subject: Species occupancy/occurrence workshop 9-12 June,
messages.subject_clean: Species occupancy/occurrence workshop 9-12 June,
messages.body_plain:
Darryl MacKenzie will deliver his four-day workshop on species
occupancy/occurrence estimation at the Centre for Research into
Ecological and Environmental Modelling this summer at the University of
St. Andrews.

The presence or absence of a species across a set of landscape units is
a fundamental concept used widely in ecology (e.g., as a monitoring
metric, species range or distribution, habitat modelling, resource
selection probability functions, metapopulation studies, biodiversity
and species co-occurrence). An important sampling issue, however, is
that a species may not always be detected when present at a landscape
unit. This will result in "false absences" causing parameter estimates
to be biased if unaccounted for, possibly leading to misleading results
and conclusions, even with moderate levels of imperfect detection.

This workshop will cover many of the latest methods for modeling
patterns and dynamics of species occurrence in a landscape while
accounting for the imperfect detection of the species. Participants will
be introduced to available software through worked examples, and there
will be special emphasis on aspects of study design. While primarily
aimed at the beginner and intermediate level, more experienced
researchers will also benefit from attending.

In this 4-day workshop we shall cover,

* estimating and modeling occupancy at a single point in time

* estimating and modeling changes in occupancy over time

* using occupancy-type metrics in multi-species and community studies

* key aspects to designing an efficient occupancy study

* available computer software with worked examples

Computer sessions take place in our modern computer classroom (attached
to the seminar room); participants can use our computers or bring their
own laptop computers.

Further details plus registration information is available at
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance.workshops/occupancy09.html

--
Eric Rexstad
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling
University of St. Andrews

messages.subject: use of Anova to compare density
messages.subject_clean: use of Anova to compare density
messages.body_plain:
Please can someone tell me how I might compare densities using Anova?

I need to establish if the density of an individual species is
significantly affected by site in addition to habitat.
I have two habitats (disturbed v. undisturbed) and two sites in each
habitat. I suspect densities of some species also vary between the two
disturbed sites.
The two habitats (disturbed v. undisturbed) can be compared using a
z-test (section 3.6.5. and 8.5 (Buckland 2001)) - is there a formula
where I might similarly compare the densities directly but allowing a 2
way comparison (Anova)?

Densities (from point counts) were calculated for individual species
using an independent detection function for each site.

Advice as to how I might go about this would be v. much appreciated.
Thankyou

Claire Mead

--
